member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Compute.ComputeParameters
member.summary: The uniform block one compute pass reads, written per frame.

remarks.para: Every compute pass here takes its parameters as a constant buffer rather than as push data: the blocks run to two hundred bytes and the guaranteed push room is a hundred and twenty-eight, so there was never a choice.

One buffer per frame in flight, because a frame still being read cannot have its parameters overwritten by the one being recorded — the same reason the geometry rings and the pose slots are per frame. A single buffer would give the older frame the newer frame's camera, which reprojects everything to the wrong place for exactly one frame and looks like a flicker.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Compute.ComputePass
member.summary: One compute module, its resources bound by name, ready to dispatch.
member.remarks: The shape every compute pass in this renderer has. What differs between them is which module and which textures; everything else — deriving the layout, building the group, sizing the dispatch from the target, rebuilding the group when the frame is resized — is the same, so it is written once. The binding half of that is shared with the raster passes, which name and gather their resources identically and differ only in what they record.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Compute.ComputeProgram
member.summary: A compute module as a pipeline ready to dispatch, with its bind group layouts derived from what the module itself declares.

remarks.para: Every compute pass in this renderer has the same shape: a layout matching the module's bindings, a pipeline, a group filled with this frame's textures, and a dispatch sized from the target. Written out by hand that is thirty lines a pass, most of it a second statement of what the shader already says — and a second statement that can disagree, which is the interesting failure: a layout naming a binding the module does not have is refused, and one that merely orders them differently binds the wrong texture to the wrong slot and shades something plausible.

So the layout is read rather than written. The library records what each module binds, at which group and index, of what kind and — for a storage texture — in what format, which is exactly the set of distinctions a layout has to make.

The push block is left out of the derived layouts. It is a binding on one target and not on the other, and which group it lands in is the backend's business: the RHI takes push data as push data and each side spends what it must on it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Compute.ImageHistories
member.summary: What a storage image held before a dispatch, for a module form that cannot read the image back itself.

remarks.para: A few modules blend this frame's answer onto what a texel already held, reading an image and writing it in the same dispatch. SPIR-V does that on one read-write image. WGSL allows read-write storage on three single-channel formats and these images are rgba16float, so its form writes the image only and reads what it held from a copy taken just before — the same values, because one invocation reads and writes each texel and nothing else touches it.

A module says which images need it by declaring, beside the image, a texture of the same name with appended (see Common/ImageHistory.slang). Both forms declare it, so they share one binding table; only the WGSL one reads it, and only there is the copy taken.

One copy per image, kept for its life and remade only if the image's shape changes: the images that need it — the surface cache's lighting atlases, the radiance cache's volumes — are made once a level.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.AutoExposure
member.summary: The eye adaptation: the lit scene metered into a histogram, read back, and eased into the exposure the resolve applies.

remarks.para: The ExposureHistogram module and its parameter block, with the host half in . The histogram is cleared, built, and copied into the frame slot's own readback buffer; the slot's previous histogram is read as the slot comes round again, when the frame that wrote it has finished -- two frames of lag, far below what an eye easing over a second can show.

The module's buffer form, counting into a storage buffer rather than an image: WGSL has atomics on storage buffers and none on textures, so this runs on WebGPU too. A device without the form stands this down () and the resolve keeps the setting's own exposure.

member.summary: The lens scatter: the scene halved six times, each level blurred where it stands, and the six summed back at half the frame's size for the resolve to add before its tone map.

remarks.para: Each dispatch has a pass of its own rather than one pass rebound six times, because a pass keeps the group it last built and builds another only when what it binds changes: rebinding one pass per level would build nineteen groups a frame, every frame, where this builds them once.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.DeferredLighting
member.summary: The deferred shading: one triangle over the frame, turning the G-buffer into lit colour.

remarks.para: The sampled form of the shading module rather than the subpass one. Vulkan can hand a lighting subpass the attachments the pass before wrote and never move them off chip; WebGPU has no subpasses at all, so the same shader reads the same texels as ordinary textures from a pass of its own. The two produce identical colour — it is one source with one line different — and this is the form both backends can run.

The shading reads a great deal -- the probe field, the atmosphere's tables, the cascades, the lamps -- and not every frame supplies all of it. A slot a shader names has to be filled whether or not this frame has anything for it, so each pass takes its slot by name, and a slot whose pass did not run is bound to a one-texel stand-in of the right shape, chosen from the module's own description of it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.DeferredResolve
member.summary: The resolve: the lit scene tone-mapped, graded and composited onto the frame that is presented.

remarks.para: The other end of the deferred pair. It takes whichever picture the frame ended up with — the raw lit colour, the temporally resolved one, or the motion-blurred one — and turns the half-float scene into the eight-bit frame a display takes, with the bloom composited in and the authored grade applied.

All three of its inputs are always bound, including for a frame that has no bloom and no grade: a shader that names a resource makes it statically used, and reading a descriptor nothing has written is undefined however carefully the branch avoids it. A frame without one binds a stand-in and the push block tells the shader to leave the colour alone.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.MotionBlur
member.summary: The camera shutter: the frame smeared along each pixel's own motion.

remarks.para: A chain of four modules sharing one set of blocks (): the colour halved, each pixel's travel flattened and its tile's range recorded, each tile dilated by its neighbours, and the gather along it. After the temporal resolve and before the bloom -- a lens sees the smeared picture, so a bright moving highlight blooms along its own smear rather than from where it no longer is.
Five images, owned here and remade with the frame's size: the half colour, the flattened motion, the tiles and their dilation, and the result the resolve reads. Half floats throughout.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.ObjectVelocityPass
member.summary: A raster pass that overwrites the computed velocity with each MOVING object's own screen motion.

remarks.para: The velocity compute derives motion from depth and the two cameras, which is exact for everything that stands still — and silently wrong for everything that does not. A running soldier reprojects as though he were part of the wall behind him, so the temporal accumulation blends his history from where he was not, and draws a trail behind him. This pass redraws each animated mesh over the velocity image with this frame's and the previous frame's transforms, writing the true screen delta wherever the mesh actually won the depth test.

Every mesh binds its preceding pose as a second vertex stream, so limb and hand motion is measured as well as rigid translation. What each frame reports is the part of a tick's motion that fell between the two frames: the drawn position is a blend of the two poses and the caller says which blend named last frame's. A mesh that does not animate reports one buffer as both streams and its pose motion is zero by construction.

It rasterises with the exact transform the G-buffer draw used, jitter and all, so the depths match, and tests GREATER-OR-EQUAL against the stored depth with a whisker of bias towards the eye, writing none. Occluded parts of the mesh fail the test and leave the background's motion alone. No culling: the G-buffer's cull state varies per draw, and a face the depth test rejects costs nothing, while a face wrongly culled here leaves a hole in the object's motion.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.OcclusionQueries
member.summary: Asynchronous occlusion queries: which objects were hidden behind nearer geometry last time they were probed, so the game can skip drawing them.

remarks.para: An object registers a query; while the geometry pass is open its bounding box is drawn against the depth the real geometry wrote, colour and depth writes off, inside an occlusion query. No sample passing means the box was wholly behind something nearer.

Results lag, and that is safe. Each frame in flight owns a query set. Its results are resolved as the frame ends and mapped without waiting; they are read when that slot comes round again. Until a result is known an object is visible, and one empty result is not trusted until a second confirms it -- a camera-edge race -- so the failure mode is an extra draw, never a one-frame hole.

A slot whose last results have not come back yet (a browser's maps can take longer than a frame) probes nothing that frame rather than overwrite a buffer still being read: the objects keep what they last knew.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.OcclusionQueries.PerFrameCapacity

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.OcclusionQueries.StaleFrames
member.summary: How many frames a hidden verdict stands without a fresh answer before the object is drawn again.
member.remarks: A hidden object is re-probed every frame, so on a path that probes, its answer is never more than a couple of frames old. A path that does not probe at all -- the direct path the vanilla preset draws through, which has no geometry pass to draw a box into -- would otherwise hold whatever was hidden when it took over hidden for good: switch from a deferred preset to vanilla and walk, and the terrain and buildings behind a fence stayed missing, the frame's black showing through it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.ScreenSpacePasses
member.summary: The two screen-space fields the deferred frame computes before it lights anything: where every pixel moved to, and how much of the sky it can see.

remarks.para: Both read the depth the geometry pass left and write a field the lighting and the temporal resolve go on to read, and both reproject against the frame before this one — so they take the same state and are built together.

The motion field is computed from depth rather than rasterised, because most of what moves on screen moves because the camera did: a static world under a turning camera has a motion vector at every pixel and not one triangle that could have written it. What the camera cannot explain — a soldier, a door — is rasterised over the top afterwards.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.SilhouettePass
member.summary: The silhouette highlight: the marked bodies' silhouettes found in a mask and laid over the finished picture.

remarks.para: Two passes. The marked bodies are drawn, each in the pose it was drawn in, into a mask the size of the screen: one channel a group, written by taking the greater, so limbs over limbs and bodies over bodies of a group merge into one silhouette and nothing counts twice. No depth test, which is what lets the highlight be seen through walls. Then one full-screen pass (Post/Silhouette.slang) finds each group's edges in a five-by-five neighbourhood and lays the group's fill and outline over the picture, premultiplied, fading towards the screen's edges.
After the tone map and before the interface: the highlight is a mark on the picture rather than light in the scene, so it is neither exposed, bloomed nor graded.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.TemporalResolve
member.summary: The temporal resolve: eight compute passes that turn this frame's shading and the last frame's history into one steadier picture.

remarks.para: One class rather than eight, because they are never run apart and the order is not a preference. The motion is dilated so a silhouette reprojects with the surface that owns it; the history is decimated where the reprojection missed; thin features relax their rejection so a wire is not rejected every frame for being narrower than the kernel; the shading is compared against the guide; that rejection is smoothed once rather than four times over; the spatial filter finds the edges; the history is updated; and the result is resolved to the output.
Each pass binds what it needs by name from the target set, which is why the whole chain is this short: the layouts are read from the modules and the group is rebuilt only when a target changes.

member.remarks:
The order is the whole of it. Every pass reads what the one before it wrote, and the two that read the previous frame — the decimation and the update — read the other half of a history pair rather than what this frame has already put there.
Its own pass because the closest-occluder scatter has to be emptied first, and a buffer is cleared by a command that cannot be recorded inside a pass. Left as the last frame had it, every frame's scatter would take in every frame before, the decimation would find an occluder in front of every history texel and reject the whole of it, and the resolve would pass the raw frame straight through.

FlashlightShadow traces against the world where the adapter can and marches the depth buffer where it cannot, and stores whether each ray got there and the penumbra its occluder implies; FlashlightShadowFilter spreads that over the penumbra by depth. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Deferred.TracedSunShadow
member.summary: The sun's shadow asked of the geometry: one ray a pixel, spread over its penumbra, averaged over frames.

remarks.para: Three dispatches and their parameter blocks (). SunShadow traces a ray from each pixel towards a point on the sun's disc and stores whether it got there and how far the occluder was; ShadowDenoise spreads each answer over the penumbra that distance implies; ShadowAccumulate reprojects the previous frames' mean and averages this one into it. The shading reads the result in place of the cascades.

Four images. The raw trace, the mask the shading reads, and two accumulations that ping-pong: the one written this frame is read as history the next. The accumulations are cleared when made, so a first frame reads zero frames of history -- the denoise then reconstructs at full width.

member.summary: The volumetric fog: a froxel volume lit once a frame and integrated into what each pixel sees through it.

remarks.para: Two dispatches sharing one parameter block (): FogScatter lights each froxel and blends it with the previous frame's, FogIntegrate accumulates the column front to back, and the shading samples the result at the pixel's own screen position and depth.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Diagnostics.StageProfiler
member.summary: Times each on the GPU, with the timestamps written by the passes themselves.

remarks.para: Timing GPU work on the host with a stopwatch measures how long the driver took to write the commands, which is unrelated to how long the GPU took to run them — so the measurement has to ride in the command stream. Here that means a query set, and a pair of slots per pass that the pass writes into as it begins and ends.

A pass rather than an arbitrary range. The RHI only lets a pass be timed, not whatever commands happen to lie between two points, because that is the only shape a browser has. It is also the more honest measurement: a timestamp written outside a pass measures the gap between passes as well as the pass. A stage that spans several passes sums them, which is what the ledger already does for a stage that runs more than once.

Why the results lag, and why that costs nothing. A query's result is not ready when the pass ends; it is ready once the GPU has drained that frame. Each frame in flight owns a block of the set, and a block is read when its slot comes round again — by which time the frame that wrote it has certainly finished. A number two frames old is just as good for judging a budget as one that cost a stall to obtain.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Diagnostics.StageProfiler.SlotCapacity
member.summary: How many timestamps one frame in flight may write.
member.remarks: Two per timed pass. Every global-illumination dispatch is a pass of its own, so an ultra frame times well over sixty; a frame that exceeds this stops timing rather than overwriting its neighbour's block, and what it stopped on would be missing from every total.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Draw2D.BackdropBlurPass
member.summary: Blurs a copy of the frame into a short pyramid the interface's frosted glass samples: each level half the size of the one before and blurred by a gaussian, so each is twice as blurred.

remarks.para: The bloom pyramid's two kernels, reused with the threshold off: the four-tap downsample halves the resolution and the separable sigma-two gaussian softens each level. A level L is at 1/2^(L+1) of the frame, so its blur in full-resolution pixels is about 2^(L+2) — 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 — which covers the design's 6-unit backdrop and 14 to 22-unit glass at every resolution. The 2D pass cross-fades the two levels either side of a requested blur.

The frame is sampled through an sRGB view, so the pyramid holds linear light: the same thing a 2D draw gets from any sRGB texture, which is what lets the glass draw through the ordinary sprite pipeline.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Draw2D.Sprite2DPass
member.summary: Everything the frame draws in two dimensions: sprites, distance-field text and the loading backdrop, over the RHI and no graphics API.

remarks.para: The three move together because they share everything but a fragment shader: one vertex layout, one geometry ring, one texture bind group per texture. Splitting them would mean three copies of the cache and three rings, and a frame that draws a sprite, a line of text and a backdrop would pay for all three.

This records into a pass the caller has already begun rather than beginning one itself. Which attachment the HUD lands on is the frame's business, not this pass's, and on the web the same code has to be able to record into the surface's own pass without knowing it.

The text and backdrop pipelines are built on first use. Most sessions draw neither: the backdrop belongs to the loading panel, and building it up front would compile two shaders that a session spent entirely in a level never runs.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Draw2D.SpriteGeometryRing
member.summary: The per-frame vertex and index storage the 2D path appends into, one ring per frame in flight.

remarks.para: Two-dimensional drawing is immediate: each call brings its own short vertex and index spans rather than a mesh uploaded once. A buffer per call would exhaust an allocation budget within a frame, so each frame in flight owns one vertex and one index buffer and every draw appends at a running offset. A draw records the offset it wrote at, so the buffers are written once and bound many times.

The bytes are gathered on the host and uploaded once per frame rather than per append. That is the difference from the mapped Vulkan ring this replaces, and it is the portable shape: the RHI has no persistent mapping because a browser has none, and its queue write is the upload path both backends share. One write per frame rather than one per draw is also the cheaper of the two everywhere.
Each frame in flight having its own pair is what keeps the host filling frame N+1 off the buffers the GPU is still reading for frame N.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Draw2D.SpritePipelineSet
member.summary: One 2D shader module built as a pipeline per blend mode, over a layout that binds a texture and takes the projection and whatever else the module reads as push data.

remarks.para: Blend state is baked into a pipeline on both backends rather than set at draw time, so the blend modes the 2D path uses are that many pipelines built from the same module and the same layout. A draw picks one; the vertex layout, the texture binding and the dynamic viewport are identical across them.

The projection size travels as push data rather than a uniform, because it is eight bytes that change with the window. Vulkan writes push constants for it, WebGPU a slice of a per-frame uniform ring; the cost differs and the meaning does not, which is the point of the RHI having the notion at all.
How large the push block is comes from the module's own reflection rather than being written down a second time here, so a shader that grows a field does not need this file edited.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Draw2D.TextureBindGroupCache
member.summary: Hands out the bind group that binds a texture and its sampler, one per texture, kept for the texture's whole life.

remarks.para: A draw does not bind a texture; it binds a group that points at one. What such a group holds never changes — a texture's view and sampler are fixed — so it is built the first time the texture is drawn and then reused. A run of draws of the same texture costs a lookup rather than a rebuild.

The image and the sampler occupy separate slots rather than one combined sampler. That is not a preference: Slang's combined sampler expands into two binding slots on the WGSL target and collides with whatever is declared next, so every module of the library declares the pair apart and both targets expect it.

This replaces the Vulkan descriptor-set cache exactly, including the part that matters most: a destroyed texture must give its group back, or a long session accumulates groups pointing at views that no longer exist.

member.param: The device the groups are made on.
The shape they are built against.

Where a resource goes when it is released. Nothing here may be destroyed where it is released: a frame already recorded may still name it, and destroying it invalidates that command buffer and silently voids every command recorded into it afterwards. Null frees at once, which is only right where nothing is in flight.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Draw2D.TextureBindGroupCache.#ctor(OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.IRhiDevice,OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.IRhiBindGroupLayout,OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RetiredResources)
member.summary: Hands out the bind group that binds a texture and its sampler, one per texture, kept for the texture's whole life.

remarks.para: A draw does not bind a texture; it binds a group that points at one. What such a group holds never changes — a texture's view and sampler are fixed — so it is built the first time the texture is drawn and then reused. A run of draws of the same texture costs a lookup rather than a rebuild.

The image and the sampler occupy separate slots rather than one combined sampler. That is not a preference: Slang's combined sampler expands into two binding slots on the WGSL target and collides with whatever is declared next, so every module of the library declares the pair apart and both targets expect it.

This replaces the Vulkan descriptor-set cache exactly, including the part that matters most: a destroyed texture must give its group back, or a long session accumulates groups pointing at views that no longer exist.

member.param: The device the groups are made on.
The shape they are built against.

Where a resource goes when it is released. Nothing here may be destroyed where it is released: a frame already recorded may still name it, and destroying it invalidates that command buffer and silently voids every command recorded into it afterwards. Null frees at once, which is only right where nothing is in flight.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Draw2D.TextureBindGroupCache.Count

member.param: The texture's handle identifier, which is what it is keyed by.
The view to bind.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice
member.summary: The interface's frosted glass: the frame drawn so far, copied and blurred into a pyramid.
Reading a frame back to the host.

remarks.para: What a screenshot is, what a save's thumbnail is, and what every capture harness the port has reads. Asked inside a frame, the answer is the frame as drawn so far; asked between frames, it is the frame last presented.

The frame last presented cannot be read out of the image it was drawn into: that image belongs to the presentation engine once it has gone out, which may still be scanning it out. So every frame leaves a copy of itself behind, recorded INSIDE the frame after everything has drawn and before it is submitted:

list.item: While somebody keeps asking -- a capture session, a screenshot loop, the renderer switch -- into a buffer the host can read, so a request costs only a wait for the frame to finish.

Otherwise into a texture of the device's own, which a request copies out on a submission of its own. One copy of the frame on the GPU is the whole standing cost of a one-off screenshot being possible at all.

remarks.para: Exactly one of the two holds the frame last presented, so a request reads whichever that is.

member.summary: The surface-cache card capture: drawing every model flat into an atlas of its materials.

remarks.para: This runs once, when a level loads, and it does not belong to a frame. The caller opens the capture, walks its list of cards asking for one page at a time, draws a model into each, and closes it. So it records into an encoder of its own, submitted and waited on at the close — the frame loop is not running yet and there is nothing to interleave with.

While the capture is open the ordinary mesh-drawing path records into that pass without knowing anything has changed: the pass it asks for is the capture's, and the pipeline it is given is the card one. What differs is the push block, which carries a model's material rather than a scene's lighting.

member.summary: The game's compute seam: the distance field, the surface cache and its gathers, over the RHI.

remarks.para: The seam is shaped the way the port's first backend was — storage buffers and images bound to numbered slots, textures to units, parameters set one at a time by name — and every module in the library keeps to one binding space so that shape maps onto it without a table per module: images at 0 to 15, storage buffers at 16 to 31, textures at 32 to 47 with their samplers at 64 and up, and the parameter block at 49 (see ). So a dispatch here reads the module's reflection and fills each slot from what the seam bound to it, and nothing about any one module is written down twice.

A dispatch inside a frame is recorded into it, in a compute pass of its own — the pass boundary is the barrier, which is why has nothing to add. Outside a frame, which is a level loading, it is submitted on its own and waited for.

The parameter block is snapshotted per dispatch, into a buffer of its own, because the game sets a shader's parameters and dispatches it several times a frame with different ones: one buffer written in place would give every dispatch of the frame the last one's values.

member.summary: The renderer the game talks to, over the RHI and no graphics API.

remarks.para: It draws both of the game's paths. The direct one is the original's: the world drawn forward into the back buffer, the HUD and menus over it, and nothing kept afterwards -- what the vanilla preset asks for. The deferred one is the remaster's, drawn whenever a scene capture is open; it reports , and a preset that does not want it declines to open one.

Two halves. The direct path is a whole renderer rather than a slice of one: every pass it needs is here, and it can be run and judged on its own. The deferred stack is the larger half, and is drawn whenever a scene capture is open.

member.summary: The cube maps a level bakes, and the state that says which one a run of draws reflects.

remarks.para: A cube is six faces of one edge and one level, filled a face at a time; names the one the draws that follow reflect, and a draw reflects exactly when one is named and known -- the reflective variant of the forward pipeline, with the cube bound in its second group. Every other draw binds the white stand-in, which no variant that does not reflect ever samples.

Stored as sRGB, like every texture on this path: the sampler decodes and the shader, told the sampler decodes, puts the encoding back, so a reflection composites at the encoding its faces were authored in.

member.summary: What the direct path is told and does not act on, and the handful of things it genuinely does.

remarks.para: A setting that is stored and then ignored is the worst kind of dead control: the value persists, the options screen shows it, and the picture never changes — so the person changing it concludes the effect is broken rather than absent, and anyone comparing two renders is comparing configurations that were never the same. The names are therefore reported through , where the shell says so out loud at start-up, and each disappears from the list on the day its pass lands.
The alternative — throwing — would be worse and not more honest: the game calls these unconditionally, so a device that threw would run no frame at all rather than the frame it can draw.

member.summary: The deferred frame: the G-buffer, the shading over it, and the resolve onto the screen.

remarks.para: Three passes rather than one. The geometry pass writes what every surface IS — its colour, which way it faces, what it is made of and what light was baked onto it — into four targets and a depth buffer. The shading pass reads all five back as textures and turns them into lit colour. The resolve turns that half-float colour into the eight-bit frame a display takes.
The shading reads them as TEXTURES rather than as subpass inputs: WebGPU has no subpasses at all, and one form that every backend has is one form to keep right.

After the shading, the forward pass: what cannot be in a G-buffer because a G-buffer holds one surface per pixel — the translucency, the muzzle flash, and the first-person arms and weapon — drawn over the lit image against the scene's own depth.

What a backend cannot run is named honestly rather than drawn wrongly: its console variables are reported as unimplemented (see ) and its pass stands down, rather than, say, a window pane being drawn as ordinary translucency -- a frame that looks finished and is not.

member.summary: Everything the direct path draws: textures, meshes, sprites and text.
member.content: The draw clip: a scissor narrowing the scene's and the frame's passes to a part of the view.
member.summary: The eye adaptation: what the frame is exposed by, metered from the lit scene.
The player's flashlight: what the shading, the fog and the first-person rig light with besides the lamps.
member.remarks: Held for one capture, as the lamps are: the shading and the fog read it and the forward pass lights the rig from it afterwards, so it is cleared only as the capture ends -- a frame that sets none has none.
member.summary: Finishing what a frame has recorded so far, in the middle of it, so it can be read back.

remarks.para: A frame's work is recorded as it goes and submitted when the frame ends, so something asked for part way through -- a capture of the frame as drawn so far, a diagnostic reading a compute result -- has nothing it could wait for. A flush submits what has been recorded, has the device send it and wait for it, and then carries on: whichever pass was open is opened again over what it had drawn, so the draws after the flush land where they would have.
It stalls the host on the GPU, which is what the callers want and what nothing drawn every frame should do.

member.summary: The volumetric fog: the haze a level is seen through, lit by the sun and the sky.
DLSS frame generation: frames generated between the rendered ones, at present time.

remarks.para: Unlike every other feature here it does not run where it is called. It runs inside the present, from what the frame tagged as living until then: the depth and the motion, the picture without the interface, and the interface by itself — so every rendered frame that wants it tags all four and the camera constants, and the backend keeps them in the layout their tags named until the present has read them.

Three states, said apart in the log. What was requested is the setting. What is effective stands down for menus, loading, pauses and cuts — frames with no continuous motion to interpolate along — and while the plugin is loading. What is presenting is what the plugin itself reports after the present. Switching it off for good unloads the plugin and rebuilds the swapchain, because while loaded the host renders into the plugin's images and pays a copy every frame even with it off; a pause only sets it off and keeps its resources, so play resumes without a rebuild.

member.summary: The glazing's draws: what a window pane lets through, and the front layer it reflects from.

remarks.para: A pane is drawn in the forward pass, after the light, by a pipeline of its own: the transmission is its tint premultiplied by its transparency, and the lit scene behind it shows through by exactly the share it does not cover. See .

Before that, when the game asks for it, the FRONT LAYER: every pane drawn again into a layer of its own with a depth buffer of its own, recording the nearest pane's world normal and distance. What a pane reflects is traced from that layer after the frame is lit; see the reflections.

member.summary: What the game's GI stack reads from the frame, and what the shading reads back from it.

remarks.para: The stack itself — the distance field, the surface cache's lighting, the radiance cache, the screen gather — is the game's, and runs through the compute seam. This is the two ends of it on the device: the frame's own images handed to the gather as texture handles, and what the stack produces bound into the shading with the numbers that say how to read it.

The handles to the frame's images are ALIASES rather than textures of the table's own: the scene's targets are remade on a resize and the card atlas whenever the capture wants a new size, while the game keeps one handle for the life of the level. Each is resolved to whatever stands behind it when a dispatch reads it.

member.summary: The mission's authored colour grade: a cube the resolve looks every displayed colour up in.
Forgetting the frames before this one, all at once.

remarks.para: Everything temporal in the frame believes this frame continues the last: the motion is measured against the previous camera, the upscaler blends its history in, the traced shadows and the fog accumulate, the occlusion reprojects, and an NVIDIA reconstruction keeps a history of its own. Across a cut none of that is true, and each keeps showing the old view for as long as its history lasts.

So a reset is one request that reaches all of them, latched until the next scene capture consumes it, and lasting exactly that frame: the motion is measured as none, the upscaler writes the frame without blending, the accumulations restart, and a reconstruction is told to reset.

member.summary: The remastered heads-up display drawn apart and laid over the frame as if projected on a visor.

remarks.para: Between and the 2D drawing lands in a transparent layer of its own, as the interface layer's does (GraphicsDevice.Layer.cs): every sprite blends into transparent black, which accumulates premultiplied colour and coverage. The compose blurs that layer into its glow with the backdrop's own kernels () and draws it over whatever the interface draws into -- the back buffer, or the interface layer of a frame drawn apart -- through Ui/HudFx.slang, blended as premultiplied "over".

member.summary: Coarse shadow maps for every lamp in the level, for the surface cache's relight.

remarks.para: Without ray tracing, the relight asked the distance field whether a lamp reached each patch of the cache. Near the camera the field is a quarter of a metre a voxel; sixty metres out it is one or two, and the wall a row of lamps is fixed to the far side of is not in it. Those lamps lit the near side of their own wall in the cache, and the screen gather bounced it onto the wall the player was looking at, in a bright patch the traced frame had dark. The lamp shadow maps answer this exactly, but only for the few lamps nearest the camera.

So every lamp also gets six small faces here, drawn once after a level loads and kept: the relight's question is whether a lamp's light reaches a patch of wall a hand across, which a map of sixty-four texels a side answers, and a static world draws the same picture every time.

member.summary: The nearest lamps' own shadow maps, for the lamp shadows marched without ray tracing.

remarks.para: The distance field a software lamp shadow marches is a quarter of a metre a voxel at its finest and is built from each model's own field, a metre a voxel for a building. A canopy a few centimetres thick that stands between a row of wall lamps and the wall beneath them is not in it at any resolution the march can tell from the wall it grows out of, and the lamps lit that wall, the ledge and the ground below through it -- where the traced shadow had them dark. The leaked light then bounced, and that bounce is what snapped as the camera moved.

So the lamps nearest the camera get what a rasteriser has always given a light: the world drawn from it into a depth map. Each map is a layer of one array, drawn through the cascades' own depth-only pass with a perspective projection out of the fitting's glass. It holds thin slabs, cut-outs and bodies exactly; lamps without one keep the field march.

member.summary: The level's lamps: what the shading, the fog and the first-person rig are lit by besides the sun.
member.remarks: Held for one capture: the shading reads them, the fog scatters them, and the forward pass lights the rig from them after the shading has run, so they are cleared only as the capture ends -- a frame that submits none still lights from none.
member.summary: Latency: NVIDIA Reflex's pacing and the PC latency markers, where the runtime runs them.

remarks.para: A frame here is one that reaches the screen. The host calls at the top of every pass of its loop, and the backend begins a frame only once the previous one has been presented — so the passes that only tick, or that leave early with nothing due, neither pace nor count. Calling the sleep once per loop pass instead once paced several times per presented frame and took the processor's frame time from one millisecond to eight.
The markers run whether or not low latency is on: they are how latency is measured at all, and the driver's overlay and NVIDIA's own tools read them.

member.summary: The picture and the interface drawn apart, and laid together at the end of the frame.

remarks.para: Ordinarily the resolve writes the finished picture straight into the back buffer and the interface is drawn over it there. Frame generation needs the two apart: it interpolates the picture without the interface (the "HUD-less" colour) and moves the interface separately, or every menu and readout smears between frames.

So when it is wanted the resolve writes an image of its own — — and everything drawn after it lands in a transparent layer. The sprites blend into that layer over transparent black, which accumulates premultiplied colour and coverage, and laying it over the picture as ui.rgb + (1 − ui.a)·picture gives the pixel the direct path would have drawn. Only additive sprites differ, and they are built to leave coverage alone (see SpritePipelineSet.LayerBlendFor).

member.summary: The mods' passes: over the lit scene between the shutter and the lens, and over the finished picture between the tone map and the interface.
member.remarks: While a pass over the finished picture runs, the tone map draws into an image of its own rather than where the picture is going (the back buffer, or the frame-generation layer); the passes read it, and the last one's image is laid where the picture was going (Post/ModDisplay.slang).
member.summary: The camera shutter, between the temporal resolve and the lens.
The motion of what moves under its own power: soldiers, doors, the held weapon.

remarks.para: The velocity the temporal passes read is derived from depth and the two cameras, which describes only what the camera did. Every draw of something that moves on its own is noted as it is drawn, paired with the same draw's transform from the frame before, and stamped over that field once the frame's depth is final. See .

A draw is paired with last frame's by its mesh and which occurrence of that mesh it is within the frame, so a mesh drawn several times pairs each draw with its own transform -- as long as the draw order is stable, which a renderer iterating its own lists gives for free.

member.summary: The one render pass the direct path has: everything into the back buffer.

remarks.para: The interface above draws without saying where a pass begins or ends — it clears, it draws, it swaps — while the RHI states attachments when a pass begins and forbids anything else until it ends. So the pass is opened lazily by the first thing that needs one and closed by whatever cannot happen inside it: a clear, a copy, the end of the frame.

A clear is therefore not a command but a property of the next pass. That is the only shape the RHI has, and it is also what a tiler wants; the cost is that a clear mid-frame ends the pass and starts another.

member.summary: The raindrops' draw: clear water that bends the scene behind it rather than a white streak.

remarks.para: A drop drawn as light of its own reads as a white scratch, whatever colour it is given: real rain is transparent, and what a streak shows is the scene behind it, refracted. So the first drop of a frame breaks the forward pass for one copy of the lit image as it stands -- every opaque surface lit, the translucency before the storm drawn -- and every drop after samples that copy through its own lens. See .
A copy rather than the lit image itself because the drops are drawn INTO the lit image: a pass cannot read what it is writing.

member.summary: DLSS ray reconstruction: reconstruction and denoising in one network, fed the raw traced light.

remarks.para: Ray reconstruction replaces the engine's denoisers as well as its resolve, so it changes what the frame traces, not only what reconstructs it. While it runs () the sun, the lamps, the flashlight, the indirect light and the reflections each fire their one ray a pixel from white noise and hand it to the shading as it came back: no penumbra filter, no accumulation, no probe grid, no spread. The ambient occlusion stands down, since the gather's own rays darken the corners it would.

Beside that colour it reads the depth and motion the super-resolution path reads, three guides of what each pixel is made of (Post/ReconstructionGuides.slang), and how far each reflection's ray travelled with the camera's world transforms -- the alternative its guide offers to specular motion vectors, which this renderer does not make.

A frame whose evaluation fails is resolved by the engine from that raw colour -- noisy, once -- and the fault is remembered: the next plan comes back as the engine's own with the reason, and the denoisers take over again. Asking for a different reconstruction clears it.

member.summary: The two ray-reconstruction inputs the G-buffer cannot give: the first-person rig's guides, and the scene's colour before anything transparent was drawn over it.

remarks.para: The rig is drawn in the forward pass and never reaches the G-buffer, so the guides built from the G-buffer describe the wall behind the hand. Each of its opaque draws is remembered as it is made -- the call, the ranges, the block it carried -- and drawn again just before the evaluation through the rig's guide shader (World/RigGuides.slang), into a base-colour and a normal image the guide pass reads where the rig stands. Drawn through the same transform and the same first-person depth range, it lands exactly on the depth the rig left, and the depth test keeps only what is visible.

The colour before transparency is the noisy opaque scene alone (Streamline's DLSS-RR guide, 4.1.11): it is how the network tells a particle or a pane drawn over a surface from a change in that surface's own light, which is what keeps smoke and sparks from ghosting. It is copied from the lit image at the first transparent forward draw; the reflections, which are the opaque surfaces' own light but are laid over the lit image after the forward pass, are laid over this copy too; and the rig, which is opaque but may be drawn after the first transparent draw, is taken from the finished image by the guide pass. A frame that draws nothing transparent copies the finished image at the evaluation, and the two are then the same.

member.summary: NVIDIA's reconstructions in the engine resolve's place: DLSS, DLAA and ray reconstruction.

remarks.para: The frame is planned before it is drawn: the host says what it wants and the output size, the device answers with what will actually run and the render size that needs, and the host sizes the scene, the jitter and the mip bias from that answer (see ). Then, where the engine's temporal resolve would run, the reconstruction runs instead and writes the same output target — so everything after it, from the motion blur to the tone map, is unchanged and does not know which ran.

Every way it can fail to run falls back to the engine's own resolve for that frame, and every reason is said once, in a line naming it: no runtime, an adapter that cannot, a size the runtime would not give, an evaluation that was refused. A reconstruction that silently did not run looks exactly like one that did not help.

member.summary: What a window pane reflects: traced from its front layer and laid over the lit scene.

remarks.para: The second half of the glazing. The front layer (see 's glazing) records each pane pixel's normal and distance; after the frame is lit, one ray per pane pixel is traced against the world where the adapter traces, or marched through the level's distance field where it does not, and resolved out of the LIT FRAME where the camera can see what it hit, out of the surface cache's cards where it cannot, and out of the traced albedo where the hit is a texel neither holds. The result is added to the lit scene before the temporal resolve.

It reads what the game hands over for its own GI: the surface cache, the distance field and the roof map. A frame missing one of them still runs, over stand-ins and a field of nought levels, and the panes then reflect the screen and the sky.
The composite is drawn rather than computed: adding in place from a compute stage is something WGSL cannot do to an rgba16float image, so the blend unit adds (see Reflection/CompositeDraw.slang).

member.summary: The resolve: the lit, steadied scene taken through the lens and the tone map onto the screen.
member.remarks: The bloom and the sun's shafts are built here from the picture the resolve is about to read, so that everything that is lens behaviour sits beside the one pass that consumes it.
member.summary: The resource seams that are not the frame's own: blits, the frame copy, occlusion queries, outlines and the temporal settings.
What the wet ground and the glossy surfaces reflect: the scene's reflection pass.

remarks.para: One of two answers a frame: a ray against the world where the adapter traces, the switches allow and the surface cache is lit; a march through the depth buffer and then the level's distance field everywhere else. Either is the Reflect module with its parameter block (), after the frame is lit and its translucency drawn and before the glazing and the temporal resolve -- so a pane reflects a road with its reflections in, and the resolve steadies what one ray a pixel finds.
The composite is the glazing's, the blend unit adding the reflection to the lit scene: adding in place from a compute stage is something WGSL cannot do to an rgba16float image.

member.summary: Snipers' scopes catching the light: stars of streaks added over the picture.
member.remarks: A full-screen pass, seven glints a draw, added with one-one blending into whatever the 2D drawing goes to -- the picture, or the interface layer of a frame drawn apart -- so it only ever brightens. The glints are procedural (Ui/ScopeGlint.slang): nothing is sampled.
member.summary: The shading: the G-buffer read back as textures and turned into lit colour, and the sky it is lit by.
The sun's shadow cascades: the world drawn from the light, once per slice of the view.

remarks.para: The game divides the view into cascades and hands each one's projection and light rotation to , then draws the casters into each between and . Each cascade is one layer of a depth array the shading compares against.
This depth runs FORWARDS, unlike the scene's: cleared to one and tested less-or-equal, because it is orthographic and the precision reverse-Z buys a perspective projection would buy nothing here.

member.summary: The silhouette highlight: what the binoculars marked, laid over the finished picture. See .
The lines the renderer says about itself: what it is tracing, what the world holds, what glazes.

remarks.para: Each is written on CHANGE, never once and never every frame. Every gate behind them opens and closes during a session -- a switch flipped live, a world and a surface cache that arrive part of the way through a mission load -- so a once-only line would report whatever was true on the first frame after a level opened and never correct itself, and a line a frame would be a wall of text. What a player toggling a setting needs is one line each time the answer moves.

They exist because every failure they describe is a silence in the picture: a reflection that is not traced looks like one with nothing in front of it, and a world without its soldiers looks like a world with nobody standing there.

member.summary: The traced sun shadow: the world fed to the backend's ray tracing, and the mask traced against it.

remarks.para: Where the adapter traces, the sun's shadow is asked of the geometry rather than of cascades. The world is built from what the frame draws: every G-buffer draw is observed with the transform it was drawn at, the first-person rig's opaque forward draws are observed where only a reflection can find them, the terrain arrives through , and each cut-out texture's alpha is kept as a mask the moment its pixels are in hand.
The structure is updated as the capture opens, from what was observed up to then, and traced between the G-buffer and the shading.

member.summary: The temporal resolve: this frame's picture and the history of the ones before it, made one.

remarks.para: After the forward pass, over the finished lit image: the camera's motion derived from the depth, the eight passes of the resolve, and a copy of this frame's depth for the next one to measure against. The resolve then reads the resolved image rather than the raw one.
What moves under its own power — a soldier, a door, the held weapon — is stamped over the camera's motion with its own before anything reads the field. See .

member.summary: The rounds' tracers, through a shader of their own rather than the world's forward one.

remarks.para: The forward mesh shader fogs every translucent draw toward the fog's colour by its depth, which is right for the world and wrong for a tracer: the original switches Direct3D's fog off for its line (0x50DCC0), and a guard's line drawn in the colour of mission 1's fog, over mission 1's fogged scene, was not there at all. It also had no blend that both laid the retail colour over the scene and raised the lit image's alpha, which the temporal resolve reads to keep a one-tick line out of its history. See .

Drawn into whichever image the frame is in: the lit image during a capture's forward pass, the frame itself on the direct path. Anything else -- a shadow cascade, a card capture, the geometry pass -- draws none.

member.summary: I.G.I. 2's water, drawn by its own pipeline over the frame or over the scene's lit image.
member.remarks: Nothing of a sheet is in the G-buffer, a shadow cascade or a card: the original draws water once, in the forward pass, after the opaque world.
member.summary: The weather on the ground: how wet the world is, where water stands, and what keeps it off.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.BlurFrameForBackdrop
member.remarks: The frame is copied into an sRGB texture the size of the screen — so the pyramid built from it holds linear light — and the bloom kernels blur it into levels in one compute pass. The levels are adopted into the texture table once per size, so the 2D pass binds them by handle like any texture. A frame the device cannot read from blurs to nothing, and the glass is drawn as its tint alone.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.ReleaseBackdropHandles
member.summary: Lets go of the pyramid's handles when it is remade at a new size; the table retires the textures.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.DisposeBackdrop
member.summary: Releases the backdrop's own resources on disposal; the table disposes the adopted levels.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.CaptureFrames
member.summary: How many frames the readable copy stays armed after somebody asks for one.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.CapturingFrames
member.summary: Gets whether this frame should be copied back as it is submitted.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.FrameReadable
member.summary: Gets whether the frame's image can be copied from at all.
member.remarks: A browser's canvas is readable only where the adapter offers it, and a frame that is not reads as black rather than as a copy the device would refuse.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.RecordCapture
member.summary: Leaves the frame about to be submitted behind, where a request between frames reads it.
member.remarks: Recorded with the frame rather than after it: the image is the swapchain's, and once the frame is presented the presentation engine owns it again.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.CopyFrameToCaptureBuffer(System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Copies the frame into this slot's host-readable buffer.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice._computeTimingLabel
member.summary: Fills every slot the kernel's module declares from what the seam bound, then records the dispatch.

remarks.para: Recorded into the frame whenever there is one to record into -- including a frame that has not opened yet, once the game is presenting. The surface cache's lighting and the distance field's clipmaps are dispatched before a frame's first draw, and the menu does that every frame: taken for load-time work, each of those dispatches was submitted on its own and waited on until the device was idle, which stalled the CPU on the GPU twice a frame and left the two never working at once -- half the menu's main thread, on both backends.
Before the first frame has been presented it is load time: submitted and waited on, so the slot past the frames in flight is always free.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.SampledOrStandIn(OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.ComputeKernel,OpenIGI.Shaders.ShaderBinding,System.Collections.Generic.HashSet{OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.IRhiTexture})
member.summary: What a sampled slot reads, unless nothing correct could come of reading it.

remarks.para: The game keeps the original's texture units: what it set on a unit stays there until it sets something else, across every program and every mode of one, and a program's slot a mode never samples still finds whatever the last dispatch left. GL did not care. WebGPU validates every slot of every dispatch, so two leftovers it refuses read a stand-in instead:

list.item: an image the same dispatch writes, which WebGPU will not also bind for sampling and which on Vulkan a sample would race;
on WebGPU, a texture of the wrong kind for the slot — a depth image on a colour slot, or the reverse — which it refuses outright.

remarks.para: The kind is only checked where the device validates it (), because only there does it matter. What a slot declares is read off the WGSL a module compiles to; a variant with no WGSL form -- the ray-query ones -- used to report every texture as a colour slot, and now takes its siblings' shapes, but one it alone declares still does. Vulkan and Direct3D 12 read a depth image through either kind, and checking there once swapped the scene's own depth out of the traced screen gather for a stand-in: with tracing on, the RHI's screen GI found no sky and no real surfaces, and shifted colour as the camera moved.

member.summary: What a sampled slot reads: the volume or the texture on its unit, or a stand-in of its shape.
member.remarks: A unit can hold a flat texture and a volume at once, as the original's API allowed, and the slot's own dimension is what chooses between them. A slot nothing is bound to reads a stand-in of the right shape rather than being left undefined.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.PresentFormat
member.summary: Gets the format the frame is presented in.

remarks.para: The device's own, asked once when this is built: every pipeline drawing into a frame has to be built for the frame's format, and the window system chooses it. A desktop swapchain here hands out an unsigned-normalised image, so the interface composites and blends at the display encoding; an offscreen target is whatever it was attached as; a browser canvas may be sRGB.

It was a constant, and a constant is what a pipeline built for sRGB and pointed at an unsigned-normalised swapchain is: refused by the validation layer, and a frame with its gamma applied twice by anything that let it through.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.CreateCube(OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.IRhiDevice)
member.summary: The environment cube every world draw binds, whether or not it samples one.

remarks.para: One white texel on each of six faces. The forward shader declares the cube unconditionally and only reads it where a draw is reflective, so something has to be bound at that group for every draw — Vulkan tolerates a set the shader never reads, and WebGPU refuses to record a draw whose layout has an unbound group at all.
White rather than black because it is the identity of the multiply it would take part in: a draw that reflects nothing and one that reflects this are the same picture.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.SealEncoder(System.String)
member.summary: Finishes what the frame has recorded so far, to be submitted with the rest at the swap.

remarks.para: Called after each stretch of the frame: every shadow cascade, the geometry, the shading, the temporal resolve and the lens chain. Finishing an encoder is where WebGPU validates and translates everything recorded into it -- five of mission 1's thirteen milliseconds a frame, one encoder for the whole frame, all of it at the swap and none of it overlapping anything. Sealed in pieces, each piece is finished while the next is recorded, on a backend that finishes off the recording thread; what is left to finish at the swap is only what came after the last seal. The compute stretches matter as much as the draws: a dispatch binds a dozen images, and those cost WebGPU far more to validate than a draw does.
A pass still open is left alone and the seal skipped: an encoder cannot be finished around one.

Nothing changes about what runs or in what order: the pieces are submitted together, in the order they were recorded, exactly where the single encoder was. On Vulkan a finish is next to free, and a few more command buffers a frame are nothing.

member.param: What the piece holds, for captures and for any error finishing it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.RecordedWorkMarker
member.summary: A marker on recorded work, which the RHI can only answer for once it has been sent.

remarks.para: The RHI times a pass rather than an arbitrary range, so a bracket names the stage of the passes opened inside it that have no stage of their own: the frame's pass, which the interface, the debug drawing and the whole of the direct path draw into. Every scene pass and every lighting dispatch is timed as its own stage whatever bracket it falls in.

A frame pass already open was timed for what came before the bracket, so while anything is measuring it is closed at the bracket's edge and the next draw opens one timed for this stage. Nothing is measuring otherwise, and then the break would buy nothing.

member.summary: Writes the geometry pass's surface block, when what it says has changed.

remarks.para: Not a block of zeros. The floor gloss is a MULTIPLY on an up-facing surface's roughness, and one is its identity: nought makes every floor a mirror. member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.Drawing2D
member.summary: Gets whether a 2D draw goes to the frame now, which it does whenever no scene is being captured.
member.remarks: Two-dimensional drawing is the interface, and it lands on the frame over the resolved scene. While a capture is open, the frame is not what is being drawn: opening the frame's pass would close the scene's and every draw after it would be lost, and whatever did land on the frame would be painted over by the resolve, which covers all of it. So the three 2D draws decline alike until the capture has been resolved, where the frame order puts them anyway.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.SetProjection(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix4f@)
member.remarks: The first-person rig is drawn without the world's jitter for the engine's own resolve, which knows the layer and never accumulates it. An NVIDIA reconstruction knows no such layer: every pixel it is given has to carry the jitter it is told about, or the rig's edges are reconstructed from samples it thinks were moved and were not. So under one the device jitters the rig itself, by the same render pixels as the world, and keeps the unjittered projection for measuring the rig's motion.

member.remarks: The lit image, which at the point the gather reads it still holds the frame before.

remarks.para: Uploaded into four volumes of its own, one per irradiance channel and one for the distance moments, in the layout the radiance cache writes: the shading reads both through the same four slots, and cannot tell them apart. A new field gets new volumes and the old ones are retired with the frames still reading them, so nothing in flight has its field rewritten underneath it.

Half floats, as the cache's are. The coefficients need nothing more, and the distance moments are bounded by the bake's longest ray, thirty metres, whose square is far inside the range; a full float volume is also one a browser may not be able to filter.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.SetPoseInterpolation(System.Single,System.Single)

remarks.para: An animated mesh in the G-buffer, and the first-person rig's opaque forward draws. The rig for a different reason: its parts are immutable meshes whose per-frame transforms carry the recoil, and the foreground layer deliberately gives them no camera motion, so without a stamp the resolve lays the old weapon pose over the new one. The additive muzzle flame neither owns the stored depth nor wants history.

Only a draw that WRITES depth may stamp, because the stamp is tested against the stored depth and a mesh that never wrote it cannot own it. The sky's cloud layers are animated meshes drawn with depth off; stamped, their far-plane depth plus the stamp's bias would beat every distant surface and write the clouds' drift over the true motion of everything beyond some twenty metres.

remarks.para: The held picture the menu dissolves from, copied inside the frame: whatever has drawn so far -- the outgoing level, resolved, before the interface goes over it -- is copied out, and the frame's pass reopens on top of it so nothing drawn is lost and the draws that follow can sample the copy.

The texture takes the frame's channel order, in its sRGB form. A copy moves bytes and cannot swizzle, and the bytes in the frame are already encoded -- by the shaders into an unsigned-normal frame, by the hardware into an sRGB one -- so sampling them through an sRGB view decodes the same light either way. A browser canvas is red-first where the desktop is blue-first, so the texture is remade in the frame's order the first time the two differ.

Between frames there is nothing this device may copy: the last frame's image belongs to the presentation engine once it has gone out. Nothing asks there -- the menu holds its picture mid-frame -- so it is left as it was.

member.remarks: A box is drawn against the geometry pass's depth, so a query is only probed while that pass is open. Anywhere else the object is left as it was rather than probed. The box takes the projection the geometry is drawn with, which on this path already is the target's clip space.

remarks.para: The selection glow, drawn into whichever pass is open: the forward pass over the lit image when a scene is being captured, the frame itself on the direct path. Anywhere else -- the geometry pass, a card capture -- there is nothing to mark and the call does nothing.

A mask lays the model's silhouette into depth just inside the near plane; then a stack of shells, widest and faintest first, draws the model pushed outwards in screen space, each asked only for the opacity the rings outside it have not already given, so the stack adds up to a falloff rather than a band.

member.summary: Tells the shading how far this frame's reflection answers for every pixel it reaches.
member.remarks: Where the reflection traces, or marches the distance field past the screen, it answers every pixel up to its roughness ceiling, and the shading leaves out its own estimate of the environment's specular there -- the irradiance it gathered, weighted as a reflection -- so the light is counted once. member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.SettleTracedWorld
member.summary: Updates the traced world from this frame's G-buffer draws, once, before anything this frame traces.

remarks.para: Called where the geometry ends -- the first of the screen GI's motion request or the shading -- so every ray the frame fires meets the world the frame drew. It used to run as the capture opened, from the previous frame's sightings: anything that moved or changed its level of detail was traced where it had been, and a surface just in front of its old self shadowed itself. With the shadow history clamped to the current frame that was a flicker -- the back of a moving truck, a far mountainside at every level of detail change.
What is observed after this -- the first-person rig in the forward pass -- reaches the next frame's update, as everything did before.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.ReleaseWorldIfAsked
member.summary: Drops the traced world a level change asked to be released, before the frame records anything.

remarks.para: Here, at the top of a frame, and nowhere later. Resetting frees every structure at once, so it needs the device idle -- and idle covers only what has been SUBMITTED. It was done as a capture opened, which may be well into a frame: whatever that frame had already recorded, a scene build naming the old level's structures among it, sat in pieces not yet submitted, ran after the reset had freed them, and the device was lost on the read (an invalid read inside a top-level build, on the way from the menu into a mission). At the top of the frame there is nothing recorded to be caught out.
A release asked for mid-frame waits for the next one, so the frame that asked goes out tracing a world that is still whole.

member.remarks: Measured against the previous frame's depth and occlusion for its history, which is why it runs before the frame state moves on. The shading is told whether it ran, and reads nothing it did not.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.RecordVelocityBeforeShading(OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Targets.SceneTargetSet)
member.summary: Records the motion field over the finished G-buffer, before anything reprojects against it.

remarks.para: The occlusion, the sun and lamp shadows and the screen GI each carry a history, and each ran before the motion existed: they could only follow the camera, and a moving car's own surfaces found their history wherever the camera said the car had been -- which is the road behind it. Derived here, with every G-buffer draw's own motion stamped over it, they can read where a surface really came from.
The depth is final for everything the G-buffer holds. What the forward pass draws later -- the first-person rig -- stamps in the temporal stage, over this.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.GraphicsDevice.RecordTemporal
member.summary: Records the motion, the resolve and the depth copy, once the lit image is finished.

remarks.para: Everything temporal measures against the previous frame, which moves on exactly once per captured frame, here, whether or not the resolve itself was asked for — so that turning it on mid-mission does not measure the first frame against the start of the level.

The motion is derived on every captured frame, not only when the resolve runs: the motion blur reads it too, and with the resolve off it would otherwise smear along whatever motion was last written, or none.

member.summary: The pipeline that draws a model into a page of the card atlas.

remarks.para: One pipeline, no variants. Every card capture wants the same state: opaque, depth-tested so the nearest surface wins, and no face culling at all — the port's meshes do not wind consistently, and a card that dropped half its triangles would leave holes in the atlas that later read as empty space.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.GBufferPipelineCache.TargetsFor(OpenIGI.Rendering.BlendMode,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.RhiTextureFormat})
member.summary: How the four targets are written for one blend mode.
member.param: How the draw combines with what is already there.
The formats of the four targets, in attachment order.

remarks.para: Additive and Modulate2X are the ground's two ways of combining with a pass before them, and on a deferred path they do not land in the same place.

Additive is one more material adding its share of the ground's colour, so it belongs on the base colour with the base pass it is finishing. Modulate2X is the tile's bake, and a bake is not a colour: the base colour attachment holds an albedo, and a bake multiplied into an albedo is lit a second time by whatever lights the frame. So it goes to the baked attachment, which the base pass left neutral and which the lighting reads as irradiance — and the doubling MODULATE2X means falls out of the blend for free, because src * dst + dst * src over a neutral destination is twice the bake.
Either way one attachment's colour and nothing else: not its alpha, and none of the three the opaque pass beneath it wrote for the same surface.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.GlassPipelineCache
member.summary: The glazing's two draws -- the transmission over the lit scene, or the front layer the reflection is traced from -- one pipeline per culling mode.

remarks.para: The glass pipeline in its transmission form. What comes through a pane is its colour, lightmap and vertex colour multiplied, premultiplied by how transparent it is and fogged by its distance, and laid over the lit image with one-and-one-minus-source-alpha — so the tint darkens what is behind it by exactly the share the pane covers. Tested against the scene's depth and never writing it: a pane that wrote depth would hide the tracers, the flame and the smoke behind it.

The FRONT LAYER form shares the vertex stage, the groups and the push block, and differs in the two states the transmission has the other way round: it writes a depth buffer of its own, so where two panes cover a pixel the depth test keeps the nearer every frame, and it does not blend. What it writes is the pane's world normal and view depth, for the reflection to trace from.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.MaterialBindGroupCache
member.summary: Hands out the bind group that binds a draw's diffuse, lightmap and detail textures, one per distinct triple, kept while all three live.

remarks.para: The world shader samples several textures, so a draw binds one group that points at all of them. A model's records pair the same textures over and over, so the group for a triple is built once and kept, keyed by the three handle identifiers together. When any one texture is destroyed, every group that named it goes.

There is no pool to run out of here. The Vulkan cache had to chain descriptor pools because a level needs one set per distinct triple it draws and a lightmap is per placement rather than per material, so the count scales with the number of objects in the level and one fixed pool is a ceiling a large enough level walks into — fatally, in the middle of drawing the world. Where the storage comes from is the backend's business now, and the Vulkan one grows its pools.

member.param: The device the groups are made on.
The shape they are built against.

Where a resource goes when it is released. Nothing here may be destroyed where it is released: a frame already recorded may still name it, and destroying it invalidates that command buffer and silently voids every command recorded into it afterwards. Null frees at once, which is only right where nothing is in flight.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.Mesh3DConstants
member.summary: The constants the forward mesh shader is specialised with, and the identifiers it declares them under.

remarks.para: These identifiers are the shader's contract, not this file's convenience: the same numbers appear in the Slang source, and a mismatch is a pipeline that compiles and shades with whatever the default was. Vulkan takes them as specialisation data and WebGPU as pipeline-overridable constants, which is the same idea under the other name — the RHI carries them as a map of identifier to raw bits.

The fog and the sun are here rather than in the push block for the same reason the cut-out threshold is: there is no push room left. They are also genuinely constant — a level's fog does not vary within a mission — so a change throws the variants away, which is why it only happens on a load.

member.summary: Whether the sampler has already decoded a colour texture to linear.
member.remarks: Declared by the stages that light in linear space; see Common/SampledColour.slang. Every texture on the RHI path is stored in an sRGB image, so its sampler decodes, and a stage that decoded again would square the curve. The shader defaults to an unsigned-normalised image, whose sample comes back still encoded, so a stage reading an sRGB image has to be told.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.Mesh3DConstants.TargetConstants
member.summary: The constants every pipeline built for the RHI carries, whatever else it carries.
member.remarks: One entry, and it is the difference between a frame and the same frame upside down. The RHI states clip space the way WebGPU does — Y upwards, which is also the way the engine's own projections run — and its Vulkan implementation reaches that with a flipped viewport. remarks.para: Which space the shader composites in follows the TARGET, because that is where the passes are blended. The original composites at the display encoding and blends there, and a target that stores what it is given — the lit image a capture's forward pass draws into — does the same: so the shader puts back the encoding the sRGB image's sampler took off, and adds the ground's weighted passes exactly as the original did.

A target that encodes as it stores blends AFTER decoding, in linear space. Compositing at the display encoding there raises every pass's weight to the curve's power on the way in, and the ground's passes, which partition to one, sum to less: measured, mission 1's direct path doubled its mean difference from the same frame drawn into a target that stores what it is given, from 5 to 10. So over such a target the sampler's decode and the target's encode are left to bracket a linear composite.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.Mesh3DPass
member.summary: How a mesh reaches each of the four pipelines that draw one: the pipeline, the material group, both vertex streams, the index buffer, the push data, the draw.

remarks.para: Thin on purpose. What is easy to get wrong here is not arithmetic but bookkeeping — binding one vertex stream and forgetting the other, or forgetting to stamp the pose slots a frame has bound, or issuing a range that runs past the index buffer — and each of those is a defect that appears as judder, or as a lost device, rather than as a failure. Gathered in one place they can be stated once and checked.
What to push is the caller's: the block a draw carries depends on which pass is running and is written by its own function, which is what makes those testable at all. This binds it and no more.

remarks.para: An inverted hull. The mask writes the model's silhouette into depth at a depth just inside the near plane, writing no colour; each shell draws the model pushed outwards in screen space and tests greater in reverse-Z, so it loses against the mask -- the glow stops at the model -- and wins against the world behind. A shell blends its colour over the picture and forces the target's alpha to nought, because that alpha is the frame's marker of world geometry and a glow is not world.
The glow goes into whatever pass is open: the forward pass over the lit image, or the frame itself on the direct path. The two have different formats, so the pipelines are keyed by them.
