member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.ShadowPipelineCache
member.summary: The shadow pipeline: casters into a depth map and nothing else, one per cut-out threshold.

remarks.para: A depth-only pass, so there are no colour targets at all and the only state that varies is the threshold a cut-out fragment must clear. That it varies at all is the point: the shadow pass must be asked for the same number the G-buffer was. A pass that cuts on less keeps casters the frame never draws; one that cuts on more drops shadows from things you can see. Either way the two disagree and the ground goes patchy along the edge where they do.

It binds the same material group the other two paths do, although it samples only the diffuse: a group is built per texture triple and used by whichever pipeline draws it, and a second shape here would mean a second group per triple for the sake of one binding.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Mesh3D.TracerPipelineCache
member.summary: The tracers' draw: one pipeline per , over one target.

remarks.para: The retail line blends its colour source-alpha over the scene, as the original's translucent primitive does (0x50E000: SRCALPHA, INVSRCALPHA); the remastered streak adds its light. Both ADD their alpha: the lit image's alpha is one wherever the frame was shaded, and what a tracer adds is the marker the temporal resolve reads to keep an effect that lives for one tick out of its history.
Tested against the scene's depth and never writing it (0x50DCC0: ZFUNC LESSEQUAL, no z-write; reverse-Z here, so greater-or-equal), and drawn from both sides: a strip is built to face the eye.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Meshes.RhiMesh
member.summary: A mesh's vertex and index buffers, in one of the three shapes the renderer asks for.

remarks.para: A static mesh is immutable: its vertices and indices are written once and never change, which is what most of the world is. A storage mesh is allocated to a capacity and filled by appending ranges — the terrain's growing pages. An animated mesh's vertices are rewritten each pose.

Where the memory sits is no longer decided here. The RHI places a buffer from what it was created for, which is the whole reason that use is declared up front, and each backend knows what its own driver wants. What does stay here is the pose ring, because that is not a memory question.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Meshes.RhiMesh.PoseRingLength
member.summary: How many pose buffers an animated mesh rings through.
member.remarks: Two more than the frames in flight. A frame binds one (current, previous) pair, so the frames that have not retired hold at most three distinct slots between them and a fourth is always free for the next tick to write. Overridable for the A/B that proves the hazard: at two the ring aliases exactly as the old pair did.

member.summary: Picks the ring slot this pose may be written into.
member.param: The frame counter.
member.returns: A slot that is neither live pose and that no unretired frame bound.
member.remarks: The current pose is never a candidate: the flip is about to make it the previous stream. Of the rest, a slot is free once every frame that bound it has retired, which is frames behind. If the frame rate has fallen far enough that several ticks pass inside one unretired frame, no slot is free; the least recently bound one is taken and the write is counted, because tearing one pose is a better failure than refusing to animate.

member.remarks: A range starting or ending on an odd index is widened to the word either side, and the neighbours it then covers come from the shadow — which is what they already hold. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Passes.ShaderBindings
member.summary: What one module has bound, named the way the module names it, built into groups on demand.

remarks.para: Resources are named rather than numbered. A pass that binds by index is a second copy of the shader's binding table, and the version of that mistake worth worrying about is not a missing binding — that is refused — but a transposed pair, which binds the wrong texture to the wrong slot and shades something plausible.

A group is rebuilt only when what it holds changes, and one it has built before is taken back rather than built again. That second half is not an economy: most passes bind a parameter buffer that alternates with the frame slot, so what they hold changes EVERY frame and flips back the next. Built afresh each time, that was a new group per pass per frame, and a Vulkan descriptor set is never handed back while any frame could still be reading it -- so the pools grew for as long as the game ran. Kept, a pass builds its two groups once.
Shared by the compute passes and the raster ones, because the difference between them is the pipeline and the recorded command, not how a shader's resources are named and gathered.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Passes.StandInTextures
member.summary: One texel of each shape a shader can ask for, to fill a slot nothing has produced yet.

remarks.para: A shader that names a resource makes it statically used, and a descriptor nothing has written is undefined to read however carefully the branch avoids it — so every slot a module declares has to be filled whether or not this frame has anything to put there. The renderer being built over the RHI reaches the deferred shading before it has a sky, a probe field or a shadow map, and this is what stands in until it does.

One per shape rather than one per slot, because the shape is the whole of what a binding is validated against: a volume bound where a flat texture was declared is refused by one backend and undefined on the other, and an array of slices and a depth texture are each their own shape again. The right one is chosen from the module's own description of the slot rather than from a list kept here.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.BottomLevelStructure
member.summary: The acceleration structure over one mesh's triangles, in the space its vertices are stored in.

remarks.para: A bottom-level structure is built once for a mesh and then referenced by every instance of it. That split is what makes tracing a scene of repeated geometry cheap: a thousand crates share one structure and differ only by the transform their instances carry.
Static geometry is built for traversal speed rather than build speed. Geometry that moves -- skinned bodies -- is built to be refitted in place instead, since its topology never changes.

Not compacted. Compaction was built once and switched off: its retirement path freed a structure a frame in flight could still be tracing, which a device fault caught as an invalid read when a fast camera streamed terrain. Should it come back, it belongs here and in the RHI as a compacted-size query and a compacting copy, retired by like everything else.

member.summary: Points every geometry at a new vertex buffer, before a refit reads them.
member.param: The buffer holding the pose this frame is to be refitted from.

remarks.para: For skinned geometry, whose vertices are not merely rewritten but rewritten into a DIFFERENT buffer each frame: the mesh keeps a ring of pose buffers so that a frame still in flight is never reading the one being written, so the buffer the structure was built against is stale by the next frame. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.HitRecordAllocator
member.summary: The traced world's material records: the buffer a ray shader looks a hit up in, and who owns which run of it.

remarks.para: One record per geometry of every live structure, in the layout the ray shader reads them through the buffer's shader handle. A structure rebuilt over a larger range set is given a fresh run of records rather than overwriting the run a frame in flight may still be reading, which is the whole of the synchronisation this needs.

A run given back is held for a few frames before it is handed out again; see and . Without that the records were append-only: every terrain page streamed in took one for good, so flying across a large level ran them out, and every structure built after that was pointed at record nought -- some other mesh's vertices, indices and cut-out mask. Its rays read the wrong mask (a tree's whole card cast a shadow) and indexed past the end of the wrong index buffer (a device fault).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.ITracedWorld
member.summary: The world as rays see it, where the device can trace them: built out of what the renderer draws, over the RHI's acceleration structures.

remarks.para: There is one only where the device offers ; a pass that wants it asks for it and stands down when it is absent, as it is in a browser.

The world is built out of what the renderer draws. A ray has to be able to strike geometry that is not on screen -- the wall casting a shadow is very often behind the camera -- so placements accumulate: every geometry-pass draw is observed, a placement seen once stays, and within the first seconds of a level the set is the whole level. Movers are traced where they are this frame. How the structures are built, refitted, pooled and kept alive until no frame in flight reads them is the implementation's business.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.OpacityMasks
member.summary: The cut-out shapes a traced ray needs, in one array a ray shader can reach without knowing which texture it hit.

remarks.para: A ray query has no per-texel test of its own. Traversal either accepts a triangle or it does not, so a wire fence built as one quad with an alpha channel stops a ray exactly as a board would — which is why cut-out surfaces were kept out of the traceable world entirely and cast no shadow at all. Giving them back their shadow means the shader has to sample the alpha at the point the ray met the triangle, and that means reaching a texture chosen by the hit rather than bound before the dispatch.

Why an array of masks rather than the textures themselves. Bindless descriptor heaps are the general answer to that and the right home for it eventually. This is the narrow one: a shadow ray does not need colour, or mips, or the source resolution — it needs one bit, is this texel there. So every cut-out texture is reduced once, at load, to a single-channel layer of a fixed-size array, and a hit carries the layer number. One extra sampled image on the pass, no change to how any pass binds its resources, and the whole thing is a few megabytes.

The cost of that choice is resolution: a mask is square whatever the source was, so a texture larger than that loses detail its rasterised silhouette keeps. For chain-link at the distances a shadow is read from, that is not visible; for a texture whose cut-out is finer than its own quarter-texel it would be. Point sampling is deliberate — the answer is binary, and filtering it would turn a wire's edge into a half-open texel that is neither there nor not.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.OpacityMasks.Resolution

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.OpacityMasks.MaxLayers
member.summary: How many distinct cut-out textures the array can hold.
member.remarks: Mission one uses far fewer than this. A texture that arrives past the limit keeps the old behaviour — it stays out of the traceable world rather than being traced with the wrong mask — and the overflow is logged once, because silently casting somebody else's holes would be worse than casting none.

member.summary: Samples a texture's alpha down to one mask-sized plane of zeroes and ones.
member.param: The source pixels, largest level first.
The source width.
The source height.
member.returns: The mask, row-major, 255 where the surface is there and 0 where it is cut away.
member.remarks: Nearest, and deliberately so. The rasteriser's test is alpha < 0.5 against a texture whose cut-out alpha is strictly zero or one, so the answer at any texel is already binary; averaging neighbours would invent values on the wrong side of that test along every wire, which reads as a fence that has thickened or thinned rather than as one that has been resampled. Where the source is larger than the mask this drops texels, which is the resolution cost named on the class — not a filter that could have avoided it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.PlaceholderScene
member.summary: A scene with nothing in it, for the frames before the world has one.

remarks.para: A shader that traces rays names an acceleration structure, and a descriptor set has no way to say "there is not one yet" — every binding it declares must be written with something legal before the dispatch. The world's own structure is not ready until the level has been drawn once and its geometry collected, which leaves a handful of frames at the start of every level with nothing to bind.

So there is always this: one triangle, far enough away and small enough that no ray of any length used here can reach it. Binding it is the same as binding an empty world — every trace misses — but it is a real structure, which is what the descriptor needs. The alternative is a second shader for the frames before the world exists, which is a great deal of machinery for two seconds of level load.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.RayTracedSurface
member.summary: One run of a mesh's indices drawn with one material, as the traceable world records it.

remarks.para: A mesh is not a material. Measured over mission one, 164 of 197 meshes are drawn as more than one index range and 143 with more than one texture, so "this mesh is a cut-out" is not a question that has an answer — only "this run of its triangles is". That is why the traceable world is built one geometry per range rather than one per mesh: a hit reports which geometry it landed on, and the material is looked up from that.

It also fixes something the per-mesh form got wrong in the other direction. A mesh with both solid and cut-out ranges was admitted whole the moment any solid range of it was drawn, which built its cut-out ranges into the structure as solid geometry — so the exclusion meant to keep wire and glass from casting a wall's shadow only worked on meshes that were nothing but wire or glass.

member.param: Where in the mesh's index buffer the run starts.
How many indices the run covers.
Whether traversal may take a hit on this run without asking. False for a run whose texture is a cut-out, which is what makes the ray shader test the alpha before accepting the hit.
Which layer of holds this run's cut-out shape, or -1 when it is solid and no mask is needed.
Which layer of holds this run's colour, or -1 when it has none. Read where a reflection struck something the camera cannot see and the surface cache never baked — which is every body in the level.

Whether this run belongs to geometry that MOVES — a soldier, the player, anything skinned. The surface cache is a bake of the static level, so no card can describe it, and a reflection must not let one try: a card's box is a slab, so a body standing near a wall sits inside that wall's box and would be resolved to the wall's baked lighting.

How strongly this run glows, as a multiple of its albedo -- the strength the G-buffer gives it; nought for a surface that does not. A reflection that stops on a lamp shows it lit rather than as the dark fitting the surface cache photographed round it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.RayTracingScene
member.summary: The scene as the ray tracer sees it: a structure per mesh, one structure over all their placements, and the machinery that keeps both built.

remarks.para: Everything that traces — indirect diffuse, reflections, shadows — traces against the one top-level structure this owns. Meshes register once and are built in the frames that follow; placements are handed over each frame and the scene is rebuilt over them. Nothing here waits on the GPU: builds are recorded into whatever encoder the frame is using, and what they replace is freed off the .

The ordering within a frame is fixed and matters. Pending bottom-level builds go first, then the top-level build that reads them, and nothing traces until both are done. The encoder's owns the barriers between them, for every backend.

remarks.para: The whole of what the scene has built, dropped at once. Everything here would otherwise be freed on the schedule the frames in flight dictate, and that schedule has no step that means "all of it". Its precondition is the one a level change already satisfies: the device must be idle. Nothing is in flight, so nothing is still tracing what this frees.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.ScratchBuffer
member.summary: The working memory acceleration-structure builds need, handed out a range at a time.

remarks.para: A build wants somewhere to sort and partition while it runs, and it wants that memory only for the duration of the build. Giving each structure its own allocation would mean an allocation per mesh held for a frame; one buffer that a batch of builds carves up between them is a single allocation and no bookkeeping, since every build in the batch finishes before the batch's barrier.

There is more than one of them, and which one a batch gets depends on what the GPU has finished. A build reads and writes its scratch for as long as it runs, and a frame is recorded while the previous one is still executing — so handing the next frame the same memory is handing it memory a build is still using. That does not fail every time. It fails when the two overlap, which is why it looked intermittent and why it never happened under the validation layers, which slow the recording side enough that the previous frame is always done.

A render graph would get the same result by a different route: build scratch as a transient buffer created inside the graph each frame, which will not hand back memory it knows is still in flight. This is that rule, kept by hand — a buffer is only reused once the clock says the frame that last used it has completed.
They grow and never shrink. The largest batch the scene ever builds is the size they settle at, which happens in the first frames and then stops.

member.summary: Which of the traced world's frames the GPU has finished, told from the device's own work markers.

remarks.para: Everything the world builds is reused or freed by age: a scratch range, an instance buffer or a top-level structure goes back to its pool once the frame that used it has finished, and a replaced structure is freed a few frames after that, because a frame already in flight may still name it. That needs a clock every backend can read, which is.

A marker taken as a frame's update begins covers everything submitted before it -- every earlier frame, whose work went out as that frame ended -- so once it completes, every frame before this one has finished. Frames are counted from one; nought means nothing has finished yet.

member.summary: The structure over the whole scene: a list of placements of bottom-level structures, rebuilt each frame.

remarks.para: The top level is cheap to build because it is built over instances rather than triangles — a few thousand boxes rather than a few million polygons — so it is rebuilt from scratch every frame instead of being refitted. That keeps the tree well-shaped however far things have moved, which a refit does not, and costs little enough that the alternative is not worth the bookkeeping.

The instance array is written by the CPU and read directly by the build, so it lives in memory both can reach — device-local where the adapter maps its video memory to the host, plain host-visible otherwise. Either way it is written in place with no staging copy, because it is rewritten every frame and a copy would be pure overhead.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo
member.summary: The colour a traced ray needs at the point it struck something, in one array a ray shader can reach without knowing which texture it hit.

remarks.para: What this is for. A reflection had exactly two ways to put a colour on a hit: read the finished frame where the camera can see the place the ray struck, or look that place up in the surface cache's baked cards. Both fail for the same thing — a body. It is off screen, because a window in front of you reflects what is behind you, and it is not in the cards, because the cards are a bake of the static level. So a ray would strike a soldier or the player and have nothing to shade them with, which the glazing route view shows as a body-shaped hole. This is the third route: shade the hit from its own texture.

Why an array of reduced textures rather than the textures themselves. The same reasoning as , which this deliberately mirrors: a bindless heap is the general answer and this is the narrow one. A reflection is weighted by a Fresnel term that is four per cent head-on, and where it is not, it is stretched across a surface seen almost edge-on — so it does not need the source resolution or a mip chain. Every world texture is reduced once, at load, to a layer of a fixed-size array, and a hit carries the layer number.

Filtered, where the mask is not. A mask answers a binary question, and averaging its neighbours would invent values on the wrong side of its test. This answers a continuous one, so the reduction is a box filter over the whole source region a layer texel covers.

Layers are returned when a texture is destroyed, which the mask array never had to do. Masks are a handful per level and the array outlived them all; this holds hundreds, so a second mission would exhaust it during its load if the first mission's textures never let go.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.MinimumResolution
member.summary: The narrowest and widest a layer may be, whatever was asked for.
member.remarks: The request comes from a cvar a player can type anything into. Below the floor a character's face is a handful of texels; above the ceiling the array is a third of a gigabyte.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.MaxLayers
member.summary: How many distinct textures the array can hold.

remarks.para: This was 512 and that was not enough, in a way that looked like anything but a limit. Mission one's pack alone is 393 textures; the interface, the weapons and the soldiers' own sets are all on top of that, and the SOLDIERS LOAD LAST — the mission's load sequence does the world, then the terrain, then the characters. So the array filled with scenery and every human in the level fell off the end of it. The player's reflection came out as a flat silhouette while the building behind them reflected perfectly, which reads as a bug in how bodies are shaded rather than as an array that ran out of room.
A thousand covers a level's pack, the interface and every character with room to spare. At squared in four bytes that is about 67 MB, which is half what the surface cache's own atlas already costs.

A texture that still arrives past the limit has no layer, and its hits fall back to the two routes that existed before. That is the old behaviour rather than a wrong colour — but it is now SAID, through the renderer's log rather than the console, because the silence is what made this cost a day.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.LayerBudgetBytes
member.summary: How much video memory the whole array is allowed to take, in bytes.
member.remarks: A budget, because the cap alone was the wrong control. A thousand and twenty-four layers is a sensible number at one resolution and an arbitrary one at every other: a level here holds well over a thousand textures, so the array ran out on mission one at any setting, and the log said so on every frame — geometry admitted after that can only be shaded from the frame and the cards, and WHICH textures win the slots depends on load order, so two sessions of the same level reflected different surfaces. What actually has to be held constant is the memory, so that is what is held: the count follows from it and from the resolution the player chose. At a quarter-megabyte a layer nothing changes; halve the resolution and four times as many textures fit, which covers the level.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.LayersFor(System.Int32)
member.summary: How many layers a given layer resolution affords inside that budget.
member.param: How many texels square one layer is.
member.returns: The layer count, never below a floor that keeps the array useful.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.MinimumTexels
member.summary: The smallest source a layer is spent on, in texels.

remarks.para: Only the one-texel placeholders and the smallest scraps. It was thirty-two square, chosen to keep interface art from spending the array before the world loaded — but the array holds a thousand layers now and hands them back when a texture dies, so the scarcity that justified the floor is gone, and what the floor was actually excluding was the level's SMALL textures: trim, pipework, ladders, the narrow strips on a tower. Those reflected as unshaded black slivers against properly shaded walls, which reads as streaking rather than as a size limit.
If it ever does run out it says so now, in the renderer's own log, rather than in a console line nobody sees.

How many texels square to store each texture at. The cost is quadratic — see r_reflection_texture, which is where this comes from — and it is fixed for the life of the array, because the texture is allocated here and nothing resizes it.
member.remarks: The layers start undefined and are never cleared: a hit record names a layer only once has written it, and a layer handed back is overwritten whole by the next.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.Resolution
member.summary: Gets how many texels square each layer is.
member.remarks: Nothing in the shader needs this. The hit shading reads the array in NORMALISED coordinates through its sampler, so the size is the array's own business and can be a setting rather than a constant two languages have to agree about.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.Texture
member.summary: Gets the array texture.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.TracedAlbedo.View
member.summary: Gets the view a ray shader reads the array through.
member.remarks: Read through a WRAPPING sampler, which the pass binding it owns, and that matters. These are world textures: a wall's UV runs to forty along its length and a cylindrical tank's runs several times around its circumference. The compute passes share one clamping sampler — right for the sky and depth tables they mostly read — so the wrap used to be done in the shader with fract, which is not the same thing at all. fract moves the sample but cannot move the FILTER: at every point where the texture repeats, the bilinear tap set straddles a discontinuity and clamps to the edge texel instead of reaching round to the far side. At the reduced resolution these layers are stored at, one texel is a wide stripe, so every repeat drew a hard line — a row of vertical marks up the side of every storage tank and along every façade in the glazing's reflections.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.WorldScene
member.summary: Builds the traceable copy of the world out of what the renderer is asked to draw.

remarks.para: A ray needs to be able to hit geometry that is not on screen — the wall casting the shadow is very often behind the camera — so the structure it traces against cannot be built from one frame's visible set. But the backend has no scene graph: it is handed meshes to create and told to draw them at transforms, and that is the whole of what it knows about the world.

So placements are remembered rather than rebuilt. Every draw the geometry pass makes -- and every placement the world renderer offers without drawing, which is the whole level every frame -- is recorded, keyed by which mesh at which transform, and kept for as long as it goes on being offered. For a world whose geometry does not move, that set is the whole level from the loading screen on, stable and complete; a placement that stops being offered (an object that moved) leaves a frame later rather than staying behind as a ghost.

The transforms are stored in absolute world space rather than relative to the camera. Relative would be better conditioned, but it would also mean every placement recorded on a previous frame carried a camera that has since moved, and the whole point is that a placement recorded once stays good.

member.remarks: The budget exists to keep a structure build from landing in a frame the player sees. Behind the loading screen there is no such frame, and the budget only stretches the time the level spends arriving in the structure -- during which anything lit once, the surface cache above all, is lit against a world with walls missing. So the shell lifts it for as long as the load holds the picture.

member.remarks: Ready says the scene holds SOMETHING, which is true from the first eight meshes admitted -- the per-frame budget -- while a level has hundreds to come. Anything that lights the level once and keeps the result has to wait for this instead: a frame count of nothing new admitted and nothing turned away for want of budget. Lit against a scene still filling in, every wall not yet admitted is missing from its shadows.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.WorldScene.SkinnedGeometryCount
member.summary: Gets how many of the traced geometries are skinned, and so refitted every frame.
member.remarks: Reported rather than merely counted. Skinned geometry was excluded from the traced world for most of this renderer's life, and the symptom of it being absent is not an error but a silence: rays pass through every soldier and through the player, so a reflection shows an empty room and a traced shadow falls where a body is standing. Nothing downstream can tell that apart from "the reflection is working and there is simply nobody there", which is exactly the confusion this number ends.

member.remarks: Separate from the rest because the ground enters the traced world by a different door () and can be absent while everything else is present. When it is, a reflected ray pointing at the floor hits nothing at all and the surface reflects sky, which looks like a reflection that is too bright rather than like missing ground.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.WorldScene.KnownPlacement(OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.WorldScenePlacement)
member.summary: The placement already standing where this one is, if any: the same cell or one beside it.
member.remarks: A draw's world transform is recovered from its CAMERA-RELATIVE model-view and the frame's rotation, in single precision, at an absolute position thousands of metres out -- so its last bits depend on which way the camera is pointing, by about half a millimetre. Matched exactly, a placement turning the camera nudged across a key boundary was a NEW placement: added, the old one expired a frame later, and a mesh doing that three builds running was filed as a mover. The traced world was rebuilt differently on every frame of a mouse movement, and every reflection, shadow and bounce read off it flickered -- a pane's reflection switching patches between the cache's light and the material's as the view shook, with the camera standing still. A key a cell either side of an existing one is that placement; nothing else of the same mesh stands within two centimetres at the same rotation.

remarks.para: This is how the terrain is traced. Its owner writes the chunks it drew this frame, at the positions the vertex stage drew them, into a mesh it hands over here; the placement goes into the moving tail, so it lasts exactly one frame like any other mover's, and the structure is built again whenever the mesh's says the contents changed — a few thousand triangles, so a rebuild is cheaper than the bookkeeping a refit would need. member.summary: Points every placement at where its mesh's structure actually is now.
member.remarks: Rebuilding a mesh replaces its structure and retires the original. A placement recorded before that still names the old one, and a scene built over addresses that have been freed is a scene the hardware faults on — so every placement is checked against its mesh's current structure before the scene is built.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.WorldScene.CompactForgotten
member.summary: Drops every placement of a forgotten mesh, and every static one no longer offered.

remarks.para: Runs immediately before the placements are handed to the scene, so a forgotten mesh's structure is never named by a scene that is built -- the same guarantee removing them one at a time gave, at one walk of the list per frame instead of one per mesh. The order of the survivors is preserved, which matters only in that the lists stay parallel.

A static placement the last pass did not offer again is dropped with them: the object has moved on, or the level no longer shows it. The world renderer offers every placement of the level every frame, drawn or not, so a still object is always re-offered and a moved one leaves at once rather than as a trail. Nothing expires after a pass that offered nothing -- a frame that drew no world.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RayTracing.WorldScene.Reset
member.summary: Drops the whole accumulated world, for a level change.
member.remarks: Through the scene, not around it. Disposing the structures here would leave the scene still holding them -- in its live set and its pending builds -- and the next frame would measure and build memory that had been freed. remarks.para: NOT bit-identical frame to frame, which is what this once assumed: the transform is recovered from a camera-relative model-view through the frame's own rotation, in single precision, so its translation wanders by about half a millimetre as the camera turns. See , which matches a key a cell either side of an existing one for exactly that reason.

The rotation is rounded to a twentieth: its own noise is around a ten-millionth, and the values placements actually take -- nought, a half, one, and the arbitrary angles between -- sit nowhere near a boundary that fine noise could cross. The position is rounded to two centimetres, coarse enough that the neighbour search covers any wander and fine enough that two copies of one mesh never share.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Reconstruction.ReconstructionCamera
member.summary: The camera as an NVIDIA reconstruction is told it: projection, motion, basis and jitter.

remarks.para: Everything is in 's convention — row vectors, v * M — which is Streamline's own, so nothing is transposed on the way across. The engine's matrices act on column vectors, so every one built here from engine types is written as its transpose.

The projection is the one the depth buffer holds, not the one the game builds. The game's is OpenGL's, clip depth from −1 to 1; the vertex stages remap it to reverse-Z (z' = (w − z) / 2), so near lands on one and far on nought. Handing over the game's matrix would describe a depth buffer this renderer does not have, so the reverse-Z projection is rebuilt from the same scales and planes.

The previous-frame transform is built in camera-relative space: this world's coordinates run to tens of kilometres, and the frame-to-frame travel is a few centimetres, so the difference is taken in double precision before anything is narrowed to float — the same reason the engine's own motion is measured that way.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Reconstruction.ReconstructionCamera.MotionVectorScale
member.summary: What the motion texture is multiplied by: it holds current minus previous, in UV.
member.remarks: Streamline wants previous minus current, normalised so ±1 spans the screen. A UV delta of one already spans it, so the magnitude is right and only the sign flips — on both axes, since the UV's Y runs down the image exactly as Streamline's does.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RetiredResources
member.summary: Things the renderer has finished with and the GPU has not, held until it has.

remarks.para: A mesh released, a texture unloaded, a bind group evicted — every one of those is a device resource that a frame already recorded may still name, and frames are in flight: the one being recorded, and however many were submitted and have not finished. Destroying such a resource does not fail at the call. It invalidates the command buffer that named it, and Vulkan then quietly refuses every command recorded into it afterwards — which is a frame that presents nothing, from the first level load onwards, with no error anywhere the renderer can see.

So nothing is destroyed where it is released. It is retired against the frame being recorded and freed once that frame can no longer be in flight, which is the same rule the per-frame rings use: begin frame N and frame N minus the frames in flight has certainly finished.
The alternative — waiting for the device to go idle at each release — is correct and costs a full pipeline drain per unloaded texture, of which a level has thousands.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.ShaderBindingLayout
member.summary: Turns what a module declares into the bind group layout entries that declare it to the device.

remarks.para: A layout written out by hand is a second statement of what the shader already says, and a second statement can disagree: a layout naming a binding the module does not have is refused, and one that merely orders them differently binds the wrong texture to the wrong slot and shades something plausible. So the layout is read rather than written, from the reflection the build commits beside each compiled variant.

What a layout has to say is exactly what the reflection records: the kind, the view dimension, whether a texture is an array of slices, what is read out of it, whether a sampler compares, and a storage texture's format and access. The last four are things a Vulkan descriptor set does not distinguish at all, so they are only ever wrong in the browser — which is why they are read from the shader rather than assumed.
The push block is left out. It is a binding on one target and not on the other, and which group it lands in is the backend's business; the RHI takes push data as push data.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.ShaderConstants
member.summary: Keeps a set of specialisation constants down to the ones a module actually declares.

remarks.para: A constant a shader no longer reads is easy to leave behind: the value is still computed, still handed over, and on Vulkan still silently ignored — an unknown identifier in the specialisation data costs nothing and says nothing. WebGPU refuses it outright, because an override is set by the identifier the module declared and one it never declared cannot be set at all.

So the two backends disagree about a mistake neither of them causes, and the disagreement surfaces only where a frame is drawn on both. Filtering here removes it at the source: what is supplied is what the module says it takes, and a constant that quietly stopped existing stops being sent.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Sky.SkyAtmosphere
member.summary: The atmosphere's lookup tables and the passes that build them: the sky's colour in every direction, how much sunlight survives to a surface, and the sky's light reduced to nine numbers a colour.

remarks.para: Two of the tables describe the air itself and nothing else, so they are built the first time this runs and never again. The other two describe the sky as it looks from where the camera stands with the sun where it currently is, and are rebuilt only when one of those actually moves.

The tables are small enough that rebuilding them costs almost nothing: the sky view is under twenty thousand texels and the harmonics are eight. What they replace is a full atmospheric ray-march at every pixel of the sky and at every surface asking how much sun reaches it.

There are no barriers here. Each pass reads what the one before wrote, and making that visible is the backend's business — which is the whole reason this can be one piece of code over two very different implementations.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Sky.SkyAtmosphere.ReadbackSlots
member.summary: How many copies of the harmonics are kept in flight, more than the frames are.
member.remarks: With one slot a frame in flight -- two -- the reader had the copy recorded this frame, which it may not touch, and last frame's, which had not arrived when the game asked mid-frame. While the sky changed it therefore waited for last frame's GPU work to finish, every frame, and holding the time scrub ran the frame at the CPU's and the GPU's time added together: forty-four per cent of the main thread spent waiting. Four slots keep a copy two or three frames old always arrived.

member.summary: Copies this frame's harmonics down to the host, for the game layer to read.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.SurfaceCache.CardAtlas
member.summary: The four images the world's surfaces are captured into, and the pass that draws into them.

remarks.para: Lighting a room from bounced light means knowing how bright every surface in it is, including the ones off screen and behind the camera. Re-shading those per ray is far too expensive, so every model is photographed once, flat, from up to six directions — those photographs are cards, and they live here. A ray that hits a wall does not shade the wall; it looks up the wall's page.

Four targets, because a photograph of a material needs four things: what colour it is, which way it faces, how it responds to light, and how far behind the card's window it sits. The last is what lets a reader tell whether the surface it hit is the one the card recorded, or something else that happens to project to the same place.
Capture happens at load rather than in a frame, which is why the whole atlas is cleared once when the pass opens and each model then takes a page of it with a viewport and a scissor.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.SurfaceCache.CardAtlas.TargetCount
member.summary: How many colour targets a capture writes.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.SurfaceCache.CardAtlas.Formats
member.summary: What each of the four pages holds.
member.remarks: Ten bits for the normal, because the bounced light a normal steers is smooth and low-contrast and eight bits there bands visibly across a flat wall. A full float for the card depth, because that value is the whole basis of a reader's "is this the surface I hit" test and it is not worth being clever about. Every target is four bytes a texel, which is what a readback assumes.

member.remarks: Copied from the lit image once a frame, just before the first drop draws: the drops are drawn INTO the lit image, and a pass cannot read the image it is writing.

member.summary: The exposure the tone mapper will multiply the scene by, one texel.
member.remarks: Written on the GPU every frame from the adapted exposure, so an NVIDIA reconstruction sees the image the player will rather than raw radiance, without metering it a second time on its own.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Targets.SceneTargetId.ReactiveMask
member.summary: Where this frame's history should not be trusted: additive effects that carry no motion.
member.remarks: Particles, tracers, muzzle flashes and rain draw over the lit image without motion vectors and mark themselves by pushing its alpha above one. member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Targets.SceneTargetSet
member.summary: The images a frame is built out of, allocated together and thrown away together.

remarks.para: A table rather than a field each. What a target is — its format, its size rule and what it may be used for — is a fact about the renderer, so it is written down once and the allocation, the resize and the release all read it. A field, a property, an allocation and four scattered lines for every one of forty images is how two of them end up at subtly different sizes.
There are no render passes or framebuffers here. The RHI states attachments when a pass begins, so a target is a texture and nothing else, and adding one costs a row.

member.remarks: The formats are the ones the renderer has always used: the albedo in sRGB because the textures are authored in it, the normal packed into ten bits a channel, the baked light in a float format because it is irradiance rather than a colour, and the lit scene in half floats because it is not yet tone-mapped.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable
member.summary: The textures a level has loaded, by handle, and the samplers they are read through.

remarks.para: One white texel is made up front and handed back for every handle that names nothing. That is not a convenience: white is the identity of every multiply the shaders do, so a draw whose texture was destroyed a frame early loses its picture rather than the frame, and no shader needs a branch saying which case it is in.

Samplers are shared by description rather than made per texture. A level has thousands of textures and perhaps four distinct ways of filtering them, and a sampler per texture is thousands of objects where a handful would do — which on some drivers is a hard limit rather than a waste.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable.#ctor(OpenIGI.Rendering.Rhi.IRhiDevice,OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.RetiredResources)
member.summary: Initialises a new instance of the class.
member.param: The device the textures live on.

Where a destroyed texture goes. A texture destroyed where it is released invalidates the command buffer of any frame still naming it, which voids every command recorded afterwards; null frees at once, which is only right where nothing is in flight.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable.White
member.summary: Gets the handle of the white texel every unbound slot resolves to.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable.NeutralDetail
member.summary: Gets the surface-detail texel a diffuse with no detail map of its own is given.
member.remarks: Not white, and the exact values are the point. A flat tangent normal is a half in x and y, since the channel stores the range minus one to one biased into nought to one; a roughness multiplier of one is stored halved, so a half again; and the alpha holds how dielectric a surface is, so opaque leaves the material's own metallic alone. Every term of the detail block folds to what it would have been, so no draw needs a flag saying whether it has a map. Stored as data, not colour, so a read returns the half it was given rather than a decoded fifth.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable.MipLodBias
member.summary: Gets the mip bias every mipmapped texture is sampled with.
member.remarks: The render-to-output ratio decides it, so it moves whenever the reconstruction or its quality does; is how a change reaches textures already loaded.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable.Rebias(System.Single)
member.summary: Re-resolves every mipmapped texture's sampler at a new mip bias.
member.param: The bias, in mip levels; negative is sharper.
member.returns: The handles whose sampler changed, so the bind groups that captured the old one can go.
member.remarks: Samplers are shared by description and the bias is part of the description, so this costs a handful of new samplers, not one per texture. The old ones stay cached: switching back is free.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable.Create(OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureDescription@,System.ReadOnlySpan{OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Bgra32},System.String)
member.summary: Creates a texture and uploads every level the caller handed over.
member.param: Its size, how many levels it has, and how it is filtered.

The whole chain, tightly packed, largest level first — which is how the engine lays a texture out and what every backend here is given. Uploading only the first level leaves the rest of the chain undefined, and nothing says so: the texture looks right up close and reads as BLACK the moment it is minified enough to pick a lower level, which is most of a level most of the time.
A name for captures and diagnostics.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Rendering.Pipeline.Textures.TextureTable.CreateCompressed(OpenIGI.Rendering.TextureDescription@,OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.BlockFormat,System.ReadOnlySpan{System.Byte},System.String)
member.summary: Creates a block-compressed texture and uploads its stored chain as it is.
member.param: Its size, how many levels it has, and how it is filtered.
The block format.
Every level's blocks, back to back, largest first.
A name for captures and diagnostics.
member.remarks: Stops where the chain runs out, as does with pixels. Each level is a row of whole blocks per four texels across, partial blocks counted whole.
